many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only

the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# ARC patterned-lattice encoding

For large grids with periodic horizontal/vertical separators and compact outputs. A lattice suggests partitions but does not establish whether output samples divider intersections, summarizes panels, encodes separator segments, or follows another mapping.

## Evidence-first workflow
1. Record each input's dimensions, divider row/column indices and colors, panel dimensions/count, exceptional values on divider lines/intersections, output dimensions, and all output cells.
2. Align clues to output coordinates under explicit candidates (e.g. panel marker/count summary, crossing samples, separator-segment values). Include absent/asymmetric clues as negative evidence.
3. Replay each candidate against every demo. Reject candidates with unexplained output cells or false predicted changes. Do not infer a rule from output dimensions or one plausible correspondence.
4. Before another demo request, state at least two remaining candidates, their different test predictions, and what feature would discriminate them. Do not request reflexively.
5. After a wrong test submission, invalidate the current rule and restart from the full demo ledger; do not repeat a minimally altered speculative output.
6. Once a rule reproduces all demos, construct the output mechanically and verify dimensions, row lengths, and every source-to-output lookup.

Continual-ARC requires exactly one allowed JSON action per turn, with no explanatory prose. Prefer evidence already available, but do not present uncertainty as validated inference.

# ARC panel marker-count classification

Use when an ARC input has a repeated rectangular grid of panels separated by full-color divider rows/columns, sparse marker cells inside panels, and a smaller output matrix aligned to the panels.

## Procedure
1. Identify full horizontal/vertical divider lines and partition the input into panels, excluding divider cells.
2. For each panel, count cells of the unusual marker color(s), not the separator or base colors.
3. Use all current-instance demo pairs to map each marker count/panel feature to its output value. Verify every output cell; specifically check panels with distinct counts.
4. Apply that mapping to each test panel, with output dimensions equal to the number of panel rows/columns.
5. Validate every output row length and preserve the evidenced fallback value for unobserved counts.

## Solved example and caution
One instance used a 14x7 grid split by divider color 6 into 3x2 panels, each 4x3; the base was 9, marker color 4, and output was 1 exactly for panels with two marker cells, otherwise 9. A distinct demo from the same task used 2x5 panels of size 4x2, base 2, marker 9, with all output values 1; panels contained either one or two markers. The test used divider 3 to form 3x3 panels of size 3x4, base 6, marker 5. Counts were [[2,1,2],[1,2,1],[2,2,2]], and demonstrated count-two => 1, count-one => 6, giving [[1,6,1],[6,1,6],[1,1,1]].

Do not blindly equate same task ID with an identical mapping or layout. Demos may vary colors, panel geometry, and observed marker counts.
